name: Retinal Disease
preview_text: In TCM, what your retina looks like - dry and atrophic, dotted with fresh bleeding, or swollen with cloudy edema - reveals the underlying pattern, and treatment that corrects that ...
conventional_description:
Retinal diseases are a group of disorders that affect the light-sensitive tissue lining the back of the eye. They include common conditions like diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, retinal vein occlusion, and retinitis pigmentosa. Typical symptoms are blurred or distorted vision, floaters, dark spots, and in advanced cases, vision loss. Diagnosis usually involves a dilated eye exam, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and sometimes fluorescein angiography to assess blood flow and leakage.
Conventionally, these conditions are understood as damage to the retinal tissue caused by abnormal blood vessel growth, leakage, inflammation, or degeneration. The focus is on the eye itself - the retina and its blood supply. Treatment aims to stop the damage and preserve remaining vision, but it rarely addresses the systemic factors that contribute to retinal vulnerability over time.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments depend on the specific retinal condition. For diabetic retinopathy and wet macular degeneration, anti-VEGF injections (such as ranibizumab or aflibercept) are commonly used to reduce abnormal blood vessel growth and leakage. Laser photocoagulation can seal leaking vessels, and corticosteroids may be used to control inflammation and edema. In advanced cases, vitrectomy surgery removes blood or scar tissue from the eye. For dry macular degeneration, a specific vitamin and mineral formula (AREDS2) is recommended to slow progression. These interventions are often effective at stabilizing vision but require ongoing monitoring and repeated procedures.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands retinal disease primarily through the Liver and Kidneys, with important contributions from the Spleen and Heart. The Liver opens into the eyes, and its channel connects directly to the visual system; it governs the smooth flow of Qi and Blood that keeps the retina clear and nourished. The Kidneys store the essence that is the foundation for all Yin fluids and marrow, including the subtle fluids that moisten the eye.
When Liver and Kidney Yin become depleted - often from overwork, aging, or chronic illness - the retina loses its foundational nourishment, leading to dryness, dim vision, and night blindness typical of chronic retinal disorders.
But deficiency is only part of the story. When Yin is too weak to anchor Yang, empty heat rises to the eyes, scorching the delicate retinal vessels and causing microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and blurred vision. Blood Stagnation - often a consequence of Qi deficiency or chronic disease - means the blood is not flowing smoothly through the tiny retinal vessels, leading to leakage, venous beading, and dark spots. And when the Spleen is weakened by poor diet or fatigue, it fails to transform fluids, creating turbid phlegm-dampness that clouds the vision, much like muddy water obscures the view.
This is why one Western diagnosis can correspond to several TCM patterns - a patient with diabetic retinopathy might have Qi and Yin Deficiency, Blood Stagnation, or Damp-Heat, and each requires a different treatment strategy.
The retina is a microcosm of the body's internal environment. By examining the tongue, pulse, and accompanying symptoms - fatigue, thirst, night sweats, heaviness - a TCM practitioner can identify the underlying pattern and tailor a treatment that addresses both the root deficiency and the active pathological factor. The goal is not just to stop bleeding or reduce edema, but to restore the conditions that allow the retina to heal and function.

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner starts by asking about your overall energy and thirst. If you feel chronically tired, your mouth is dry, and your vision is blurry without much redness or pain, Qi and Yin Deficiency is the likely root. The tongue will look pale with a thin coating, and the pulse will feel thready and slightly rapid - both signs that Qi and Yin are too weak to nourish the eyes properly.
When the deeper reserves of the body are depleted, Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency takes center stage. The practitioner will listen for complaints of dim vision, especially at night, and dry, gritty eyes. A dark-red tongue with little or no coating and a thready pulse confirm that the eyes are not receiving the cooling, moistening Yin fluids they need to see clearly.
If Yin is too weak to anchor Yang, Empty-Heat caused by Yin Deficiency rises to disturb the eyes. Here the practitioner looks for signs of heat without an infection: redness, a burning sensation, or a tendency toward tiny retinal bleeds. The tongue is typically red with a scanty coating, and the pulse is thready and rapid, revealing that the heat comes from a deficiency rather than a true fire.
As retinal disease progresses, blood flow can become sluggish and congeal into Blood Stagnation. The practitioner will examine the back of your eye for hemorrhages, microaneurysms, or twisted veins. They will also check your tongue for a dark-purple color or stasis spots, and feel for a choppy or wiry pulse. A history of sharp, fixed pain around the eye strongly supports this pattern.
When turbid fluids build up, Damp-Phlegm clouds the eye’s delicate network. The practitioner will ask whether your eyelids feel heavy or your vision seems misty, and will look for retinal edema or soft exudates. A swollen tongue with a greasy coating and a slippery pulse are classic signs that phlegm-dampness is obstructing the eye’s collaterals.
Damp-Heat combines stickiness with inflammation. The practitioner suspects this pattern when macular edema or yellowish exudates appear alongside a yellow, greasy tongue coating and a rapid, slippery pulse. You might also notice systemic clues like a heavy body, poor appetite, or a bitter taste in your mouth, which help distinguish it from simple Damp-Phlegm.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork and prolonged mental strain, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Excessive screen time, Hot, dry weather or saunas, Emotional stress and frustration
patterns.better_with: Adequate sleep and daytime rest, Warm, nourishing soups and congee, Gentle walking or tai chi, Cool, humidified rooms, Regular screen breaks
patterns.why_this_happens: The retina depends on a steady supply of Qi and Yin to stay clear and moist. Qi moves blood and nutrients upward to the eyes, while Yin provides the cooling, lubricating fluids that keep the retinal tissue healthy. When both are depleted-often from overwork, chronic stress, or prolonged illness-the eyes become undernourished and dry, leading to blurred vision, floaters, and a sensation of grittiness. The deficiency also leaves the delicate blood vessels in the retina fragile and prone to tiny leaks, which can appear as microaneurysms or small hemorrhages.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body, thin or absent dry coating, possibly cracked. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Yin are the body's energy and coolant. Overwork and stress burn through Qi, while spicy foods and dry heat consume Yin, leaving the eyes undernourished and dry. Rest and gentle movement allow Qi to rebuild, and moistening foods and fluids replenish Yin. By protecting these two resources, the eyes receive the steady, moist nourishment they need to stay clear and comfortable.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid pushing through exhaustion-your eyes need the same recharge your body does. Eat warm, moistening foods like congee, stewed pears, and soups made with yam, goji berries, and a little ginger. Steer clear of spicy, fried, or drying foods that burn up Yin. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps Qi circulate without draining it, and taking screen breaks every 20 minutes protects your eye fluids.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Liver opens into the eyes, and the Kidneys store the essence that nourishes them. When Liver and Kidney Yin become depleted, the eyes lose their moisture and foundational nourishment. This leads to the dryness, dim vision, and night blindness typical of chronic retinal disorders.
Without enough Yin to anchor Yang, a subtle deficiency heat can also arise, making the retinal tissues more fragile and prone to gradual visual decline.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, and often wiry; the left Chi (Kidney) position feels weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, moistening energy. Late nights, overwork, and eye strain burn through Yin, leaving the eyes dry and undernourished. Spicy foods and hot environments generate heat that further depletes fluids. Rest, moistening foods, and a calm environment allow the body to conserve and rebuild Yin, directly soothing the eyes and stabilizing vision.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, Yin-nourishing foods like goji berries, mulberries, black sesame, pears, and cucumber. Avoid spicy, fried, or overly heating foods that dry up fluids. Go to bed early, especially in winter, and avoid late-night screen time, which drains Yin further. Gentle eye exercises and regular breaks from reading can help preserve precious eye moisture.

patterns.better_with: Gentle movement and walking, Warm eye compress, Restful sleep, Light, easily digested meals
patterns.why_this_happens: Blood Stagnation means the blood is not flowing smoothly through the tiny vessels that nourish the retina. Over time, this sluggish circulation causes the vessel walls to weaken and leak, leading to retinal hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and venous beading. The pooled, stagnant blood then obstructs vision, creating dark spots, floaters, or even a curtain-like shadow in the visual field.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩, Sè) or wiry (弦, Xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stasis means the blood is thick and slow-moving. Cold, inactivity, and stress all cause things to congeal and stagnate further, while warmth, gentle movement, and relaxation encourage blood to flow freely again. Spicy and greasy foods generate heat and dampness that can make the blood even more sluggish, so a clean, light diet is essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small amounts of blood-moving foods like hawthorn berries, black fungus, and turmeric. Avoid heavy, greasy meals and excessive cold drinks, which can congeal blood. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps keep circulation active, but avoid eye strain from prolonged screen time.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weakened by poor diet, fatigue, or chronic illness, it fails to transform fluids. These fluids thicken into a cloudy, heavy substance called Phlegm-Dampness. Instead of nourishing the eyes, this turbid dampness rises and clouds the clear vision, just as muddy water obscures the view through a window. The retina becomes waterlogged, leading to swelling, exudates, and the sensation of heaviness around the eyes.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen, often with scalloped edges (teeth marks); the coating is thick, white, and greasy, looking almost oily. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), like beads rolling under the fingers, sometimes soggy in the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Phlegm forms when the Spleen's digestive fire is too weak to transform fluids, so heavy, damp, and cold foods add more turbidity. Dry, warm foods and gentle movement help the Spleen recover its transforming function, just as sunlight clears a fog. Moist environments and inactivity allow dampness to settle and thicken, clouding the retinal tissues.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Phlegm-Dampness thrives on dairy, sugar, and greasy or fried foods, so aim for a light, warm, and easily digested diet centered on cooked grains and vegetables. Gentle, consistent exercise like walking helps the Spleen move Qi and transform Dampness. Avoid eating late at night or overeating, which overwhelms the Spleen and creates more turbidity.

patterns.why_this_happens: Damp-Heat brews within the body when rich, sweet, or greasy foods overwhelm the Spleen's ability to transform fluids, creating a turbid, hot pathogenic factor. This sticky pathogen can ascend along the channels to the eyes, where it obstructs the fine collaterals that nourish the retina. The result is fluid accumulation (macular edema), yellowish exudates, and a blurry, heavy vision that mirrors the sluggish, sticky sensation felt throughout the body.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body with a yellow, greasy coating that is difficult to scrape off. Pulse: Soggy-rapid (Ru Shu) or slippery-rapid (Hua Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat forms when the Spleen is overwhelmed by rich, heavy foods and a damp environment, creating a sticky, hot pathogen that travels upward to the eyes. A light, bland diet and dry surroundings starve the pathogen, while gentle movement helps the Spleen transform and transport fluids, gradually clearing the turbid obstruction from the retinal collaterals.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and very sweet foods, as well as dairy and alcohol, all of which generate Dampness and Heat. Base meals around lightly cooked vegetables, Job's tears, mung beans, and cucumber to drain Dampness. Keep living spaces dry and well-ventilated, and incorporate gentle daily movement to keep Qi and fluids circulating.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture improve my vision?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is not a quick fix for retinal disease, but it can play a valuable role in supporting eye health. By stimulating points around the eyes and on the body, acupuncture aims to improve local blood flow, reduce inflammation, and regulate the autonomic nervous system. Many patients report that their vision feels clearer or less strained after a series of treatments, and some notice a reduction in floaters or eye fatigue. However, acupuncture alone is rarely sufficient for advanced retinal disease - it works best as part of a comprehensive plan that includes herbal medicine, dietary changes, and conventional monitoring.

faqs.question: Will Chinese herbs interact with my eye injections or other medications?
faqs.answer: Herbal formulas for retinal disease are generally safe to combine with anti-VEGF injections and other standard treatments, but it is essential that both your ophthalmologist and TCM practitioner know everything you are taking. Some herbs used for Blood Stagnation - such as Dan Shen (Salvia) or Chuan Xiong (Ligusticum) - have mild antiplatelet effects and could theoretically increase the risk of bleeding if you are also on blood thinners like warfarin or aspirin. Your TCM practitioner can adjust the formula accordingly. Never stop or change your conventional eye treatments without consulting your ophthalmologist; TCM is used as a complementary support, not a replacement.

faqs.question: How long before I notice a difference?
faqs.answer: Most patients begin to notice subtle improvements in eye comfort - less dryness, less strain - within the first 2-4 weeks of herbal treatment. Changes in visual acuity or a reduction in floaters and bleeding tend to take longer, often 2-3 months of consistent treatment. Chronic retinal conditions that have developed over years require patience; the goal is to stabilize the retina and slow progression, and this is assessed through regular OCT scans and eye exams rather than day-to-day fluctuations in vision. A TCM practitioner will typically re-evaluate your pattern and adjust the formula every 4-6 weeks to keep progress moving.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for diabetic retinopathy?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be a safe and beneficial complement to standard diabetic eye care. The key is that your blood sugar must be well-monitored, and you should not stop any prescribed diabetes medications or insulin without your doctor's guidance. Herbal formulas for diabetic retinopathy often include herbs that support Qi and Yin, invigorate blood, and reduce dampness - all of which can help protect the retinal vessels from further damage. Because some herbs may influence blood glucose or interact with medications, it is crucial that your TCM practitioner is experienced in diabetic care and communicates with your endocrinologist.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays an important role in TCM treatment for retinal disease. In general, you will be advised to avoid greasy, fried, and overly sweet foods that create dampness and heat - these can cloud vision and promote retinal edema. Instead, favor leafy green vegetables, goji berries, carrots, blueberries, and moderate amounts of fish rich in omega-3 fatty acids. Staying well-hydrated and avoiding alcohol and smoking are also crucial. Your practitioner may give you more specific dietary guidance based on your pattern - for example, someone with Damp-Heat may need to avoid spicy and rich foods, while someone with Yin Deficiency benefits from moistening foods like pears and tofu.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse retinal damage?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot regrow retinal tissue that has been destroyed, but it can often help preserve existing vision and slow further damage by improving the internal environment. In early stages or when damage is primarily functional (like edema or mild bleeding), TCM may help the retina recover more fully. The focus is on stopping the progression and maximizing the function of the healthy tissue that remains. Many patients find that their vision stabilizes and that they experience fewer acute episodes after starting TCM treatment, which is a meaningful outcome in chronic retinal disease.

research.title: Neuroprotective effects of traditional Chinese medicine formulas in animal models of retinal degenerative diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the neuroprotective effects of TCM formulas in animal models of retinal degenerative diseases. It found that formulas like Bu Yang Huan Wu decoction and Qi-Shen-Yi-Qi pills significantly upregulated neurotrophic factors (BDNF, CNTF), downregulated glial activation markers, and improved retinal function as measured by electroretinogram. The study supports the traditional use of these formulas for retinal protection.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Neuroprotective effects of traditional Chinese medicine formulas in animal models of retinal degenerative diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Pharmacol. 2025. PMC12819594.

research.title: Clinical observations and mechanistic insights of traditional Chinese medicine in the management of diabetic retinopathy
research.description: This review summarized clinical studies on TCM for diabetic retinopathy, reporting that herbal formulas containing Scutellaria baicalensis, Lycium barbarum, and Salvia miltiorrhiza improved visual acuity, reduced retinal vascular leakage, and decreased microvascular lesion counts. The paper also discussed mechanisms involving anti-oxidative and anti-apoptotic pathways, providing a bridge between clinical outcomes and laboratory findings.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Clinical observations and mechanistic insights of traditional Chinese medicine in the management of diabetic retinopathy. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. 2024. PMC11210421.
